PROFILE_FINDING: Per-rank profiling of the 122B pipeline shows each stage's GPU step at 33–34 ms median, which would be ~105 ms per token (9.5 tok/s), but 250–550 ms stalls on 40–50% of steps on every rank. The stall reproduces standalone whenever the iGPU idles ~70 ms between steps and disappears when it is kept busy; a 5 ms keep-alive inference during the network waits removes it. With a 2 ms keep-alive (or 5 ms plus a pinned clock), the 122B runs at 10.5 tok/s on the same three NUCs, 3.3x the baseline and 18x the as-shipped memory window.
SPEC_FINDING_TITLE: Speculative decoding does not pay on these GPUs: prompt lookup costs 35% on the whole 35B, n-gram speculation halves the staged 35B
SPEC_FINDING: OpenVINO GenAI's prompt-lookup path (continuous batching) drops the whole 35B from 47 to 31–32 tok/s and doubles TTFT; a draft model is refused on VLM-layout exports, which every Qwen3.6 IR here is. In the staged engine, greedy n-gram speculation with DeltaNet state snapshot/rollback runs the single-box 35B at 14–15 tok/s against 31.6 plain: 2–20% draft acceptance and 120 ms per state snapshot. On the all-local 122B the same path drops 2.8–3.3 tok/s to 1.5–1.7 (acceptance 14–23%), because every rollback is paid on all three ranks in sequence. Output parity with plain decoding held on 4 of 6 outputs; the rest differ by a character or two (f16 verify-vs-decode).
CLOCK_FINDING_TITLE: GPU clocks are not the limit: pinning the iGPU at 2.5 GHz or raising the OpenVINO queue priority changes nothing
CLOCK_FINDING: During 122B decode the iGPU bounces between 100 and 2500 MHz (median 1450). Pinning it at 2500 MHz through Level Zero Sysman, or compiling with GPU_QUEUE_THROTTLE/PRIORITY=HIGH, leaves the 122B at 1.4–3.2 tok/s and the whole 35B on a NUC at 33 tok/s. The Intel graphics power plan was already Maximum Performance.

SPEC_SECTION:
Two kinds were added and measured. For the whole model, OpenVINO GenAI's own speculative paths (prompt lookup, and FastDraft with a separate draft model) were enabled through the runtime's --prompt-lookup / --draft-model flags; GenAI 2026.4.1 refuses them with prefix caching on, so the shim now passes a scheduler config with prefix caching disabled for those pipelines. For the staged pipeline engine, greedy n-gram (prompt-lookup) speculation was implemented from scratch on branch ecg/spec-decode: the head drafts up to k tokens from n-gram matches in the prompt and generated text, the chain verifies them in one T=k+1 pass (the last stage now emits logits for every position, cascadia shard --full-logits), rank 0 accepts the longest matching prefix, and because the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state cannot be rewound, every rank snapshots its DeltaNet variables before the verify pass and, on a partial accept, restores them, masks the rejected cache slots and re-feeds the accepted tokens. New wire frames VERIFY / TOKENS / COMMIT carry this through the pipeline.

Across three ranks one verify step costs a 0.37 s DeltaNet snapshot, a 0.73 s verify pass, a 0.75 s restore and a 0.84 s re-feed, against a 0.33 s plain token; the pipeline multiplies every rollback cost by its depth.

The staged implementation is correct to the extent greedy speculation can be on this export: short outputs are byte-identical to plain decoding, the longer ones differ by one or two characters, the same f16 near-tie behaviour the surgery documents for any T>1 pass versus T=1 decode on the DeltaNet scan. It is not a win on this hardware for two structural reasons: prompt-lookup drafts rarely match the model on prose and telemetry (2–20% accepted), and the recurrent state makes rollback expensive (a snapshot/restore round trip costs more than three plain tokens). A learned draft (the MTP head that ships in these IRs, or a 0.8B draft on a text-only export) would raise acceptance, but the rollback cost stays unless the verify can run on a cloned state; that is the next experiment, not this one. The flags remain in the branch, off by default.

During 122B decode the iGPU's actual frequency bounces between 100 and 2,500 MHz (median 1,450 on alpha, 1,750 on beta), the signature of a GPU that is idle most of the time. Three interventions were measured on the all-local 122B and on the whole 35B on a NUC, all with every stage resident:

Clock state is a symptom, not the cause: forcing the clock high does not shorten the stalls, and the whole 35B, which keeps its GPU 98% busy, gains nothing either.

Where a 122B token's time goes

The runtime branch adds per-token instrumentation (CASCADIA_QWEN36_PROFILE=1: embed, per-stage set/infer/output, transport wait, sampling; and an OpenVINO per-op dump with PERF_COUNT). On the all-local 122B it reports, per rank and decode step:

Measure (per rank, per step)p50p95
Stage inference (16 layers, 20–25 GB resident)33–34 ms250–550 ms
Input copy / output copy / sampling0.07 / 0.2 / 0.3 ms<1 ms
Wire (frame on the 2.5 GbE hop)1.7 ms2–11 ms
Waiting for the other two ranks68–70 ms540–670 ms

The medians add up to a 105 ms token (9.5 tok/s); the measured 330 ms comes from the tails. A standalone OpenVINO loop on one stage never stalls (300 steps, p99 57 ms, with or without a kernel cache) until a 70 ms pause is inserted between steps, which the pipeline naturally has while the other two ranks work: then 16% of steps take ~570 ms, pinned clock or not. Filling the pause with a 1.7 ms keep-alive inference every 5 ms removes the stalls (p99 68 ms). The fix is in the engine as CASCADIA_QWEN36_GPU_KEEPALIVE_MS: each rank keeps its device busy with a tiny model while it waits on the network. Measured on the all-local 122B:

A 5 ms keep-alive removes the stalls but lets the frequency governor settle low between the tiny kernels (the last rank's step doubles; at 25 ms every step runs slow); pinning the clock alone (G1) changed nothing because the idle penalty dominated. Either a 2 ms keep-alive on its own or 5 ms with the clock pinned gives the token its median cost back: 3.3x the baseline on the same hardware, and the per-step distribution is now tight enough (p95 within 4% of p50) that the remaining cost is the kernel time itself. The full protocol with the 2 ms keep-alive (D3k): 10.5–10.7 tok/s on every prompt length, steady loop 10.6 tok/s, TTFT 0.62 / 5.5 / 41.3 s, 58 W for the chain at 16–20 GB/s of DDR traffic per box (0.18 tok/J, against 24 W and 0.12 tok/J when it stalled), GSM8K-20 17/20 with the same three truncations in 9.7 minutes instead of 41. The busy counters now read 93–95% per GPU because the keep-alive kernels fill the waits; the real work per token is unchanged.

Of the 51 ms standalone step, OpenVINO's per-op profile accounts for 18–22 ms of kernel time (149 compressed matmuls 13–17 ms, transposes 2.4 ms, 12 Gated DeltaNet ops 1.1 ms; the fused MoE experts are not attributed), so roughly 30 ms per step is the plugin's host-side dispatch across ~1,100 nodes of a dynamic-shape graph. The first requests after a load are slower still (14–18 s for 16 tokens) while kernels are specialised for new prompt lengths; a persistent OpenVINO cache directory does not change the steady-state step.
ECG_EXTRA:
• Run the pipeline ranks with the GPU keep-alive on (CASCADIA_QWEN36_GPU_KEEPALIVE_MS=2) wherever a stage spends most of its time waiting on other boxes; it took the all-local 122B from 3 to 10.5 tok/s, and it costs nothing when a rank is not waiting. Do not spend effort on GPU clock settings.
  • Leave speculative decoding off on Panther Lake iGPUs for these models. Prompt lookup costs a third of the whole model's speed and n-gram speculation halves the staged engine; the DeltaNet rollback cost and low n-gram acceptance decide it. Revisit only with the MTP head or a text-only draft export.
